steps.title: What a fusion is, and where this sits
steps.body:
This is one of the two **fusions** set works; the other is Esperanza Spalding's *Samba Em Preludio*, which you meet later. A **fusion** is music that brings together two or more distinct styles so that both remain audible.

*Release* fuses three: **African**, **Celtic** and **Western dance** music. That is the sentence to build every answer on, because almost every question comes back to it. When you name a device, say which tradition it belongs to.

Section B can set this against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, so you compare by element with both pieces in every paragraph.

steps.title: The facts to know cold
steps.body:
- Afro Celt Sound System was originally formed by the guitarist **Simon Emmerson in 1995**, and has featured many guest artists since.
- They record for **Real World Records**, the label founded by **Peter Gabriel**, formerly of Genesis, and have played World Music festivals including **WOMAD**.
- Their first album, ***Volume 1: Sound Magic***, was recorded in **one week** and released in **1996**, reaching **number 15** in the 1997 *Billboard* Top World Music Albums.
- *Volume 2: Release* was put on hold after the death of a core member, **Jo Bruce**, son of Cream's bass player Jack Bruce. **Sinéad O'Connor** stepped in and wrote the lyrics to the track that became *Release*.
- The album was released on **25 January 1999**.
- In **2000** the group was **nominated for a Grammy Award** in the Best World Music category.

Volume 1: Sound Magic, recorded in a week, 1996; number 15 in the 1997 Billboard Top World Music Albums

steps.title: The instruments, tradition by tradition
steps.body:
Learn the instruments in their three groups; a question that asks you to name an African or a Celtic instrument is a free mark if you have.

- **African**: the **kora**, a West African harp-lute, and the **talking drum**.
- **Celtic**: the **hurdy-gurdy**, **uilleann pipes** (Irish bellows-blown bagpipes), **bodhrán** (a frame drum), **fiddle**, **whistle** and **accordion**.
- **Western dance**: male and female **vocals**, **synthesisers** (string pad, soft pad, bells, string bass), **breath samples**, **drum machine**, **electric piano**, **shaker** and **tambourine**.

The playing techniques to know are **glissando** (sliding), **ornamentation**, **double stopping** (two strings bowed at once, on the fiddle) and **open and closed hi-hat**.

One word covers how most of it is put together: **looping**. Much of the piece is built from short recorded patterns repeated and layered.

steps.title: Structure: verses with no chorus
steps.body:
There is a distinct **verse form**, and the thing to notice is what is missing. The piece has an **intro**, **solos**, **breaks** and an **outro**, it contains **three verses**, and it has **no choruses at all**.

That is the exam's favourite question on this set work, because pop-song habits make students write *chorus* without checking.

The **intro** is worth knowing in detail. It starts with a **drone** on two different synth tones, **hard-panned left and right**, both filtered with **low pass filters**. A low pass filter sweeps through the frequencies, removing and then adding the higher harmonics while always keeping the fundamental. The filtering is timed so that **when the left is adding treble, the right is removing it**, and the other way round. It **begins** in **free time** and fades in gradually, and the texture thickens by **layering**: talking drum, then a synth strings drone, then spoken vocal samples. The **bodhrán, shaker and drum machine** then bring in the steady tempo, still inside the intro.

male vocal sings a variation of verse 1; a busier drum pattern; fiddle with double stopping, accents and triplets
uilleann pipes, then whistle an octave higher in running semiquavers; then low whistle, more elaborate, with demisemiquavers
female then male vocal, with hurdy-gurdy and pipes underneath: polyphonic; a new synth sample holds one chord per bar
bass and a busier drum part return; two electric piano loops, then a hurdy-gurdy loop and a pipe loop in heterophony
the bass drops out and a fiddle loop returns; the electric pianos come back as everything else falls away, and the music fades

steps.title: Loops, layering and the studio
steps.body:
Much of *Release* is made from **looping**: short patterns recorded once and repeated. The music moves forward by **adding and removing loops**, not by modulating.

Follow one thread through the piece and you can hear it:

- a **bass loop** enters at the end of verse 1 with a riff on just **two notes, C and B flat**, which gives the music a **modal** quality
- the bass loop **drops out** during the solos, then returns for the build
- in the build, an **electric piano** plays a syncopated two-note melody (**F and G**) over a semiquaver chordal and arpeggio accompaniment, with a **second electric piano** oscillating between **E flat and F**
- in the **outro**, the bass drops out and a fiddle loop returns; at the very end the two electric piano loops come back as everything else falls away

The studio is audible throughout. **Reverb** is very obvious on the whole track, there are **breath samples** and **spoken vocal samples**, and a short flute effect in verse 1 uses **delay**, that is, echoes.

steps.title: Melody and the two voices
steps.body:
The vocal writing is worth a question on its own.

- The lyrics include **nonsense syllables**, and there are some **spoken** parts as well as sung ones.
- The main verse is **syllabic**: roughly one note per syllable.
- Phrases are **short** and the writing is **repetitive**.
- The **female** vocal has a **limited range, a 6th**. The **male** vocal is wider, a **13th**.
- The opening female vocal gives a **sense of improvisation**.
- Ornaments include **glissando** (sliding) and **acciaccatura** (a crushed note).

Those two ranges are a gift in a comparison question: one voice deliberately narrow, the other wide.

steps.title: Harmony, tonality, rhythm and metre
steps.body:
**Harmony and tonality.** The music is **diatonic** and in the key of **C minor**, but it is also **modal**, and the two-note bass riff is what gives it that flavour. Chord sequences are **repetitive**, the **harmonic pulse is slow**, and there is a **drone**. There are **extended chords**, sevenths and ninths, and a **hint of chromaticism**: listen for the **low synth strings rising chromatically** at the end of verse 1 and again in verses 2 and 3.

**Rhythm and metre.** The intro **begins** in **free time**; a steady tempo is established later in the intro, when the bodhrán, shaker and drum machine enter. The metre is **simple quadruple**. The semiquavers are **slightly swung**, which is what gives the track its lilting, relaxed feel. Also listed are **syncopation**, **triplets**, **sextuplets**, **accents**, **rhythmic ostinato**, **loops**, **riffs**, short rhythmic phrases and **2- and 4-bar phrases**.

steps.title: Going deeper: texture, and writing about a fusion
steps.body:
**Name the texture and say where.** The texture is **constantly changing**, and there are three kinds to name:

- **homophonic**, the main texture: the female vocal over simple chords in verse 1
- **polyphonic**, in verse 3, where the hurdy-gurdy and the uilleann pipe solo play underneath the main vocals
- **heterophonic**, where a new uilleann pipe loop decorates the hurdy-gurdy line in the build, and again in the outro

**Heterophonic** is the one that separates a grade 9 from a grade 7. It means two or more performers playing **versions of the same melody at the same time**, one plain and one decorated. It is not the same as polyphonic, where the lines are independent.

**Writing about a fusion.** Never list instruments. For each point, say **which tradition** the device comes from and **what it does to the sound**. *Pipes and whistle play the solos, a Celtic sound, over a drum machine and looped bass from Western dance, so the two traditions are heard at once rather than in turn.* That sentence is worth more than a paragraph of names.

questions.prompt: Explain how Afro Celt Sound System combine three musical traditions in *Release*.
questions.solution: Devices tied to their tradition and their effect. Celtic: uilleann pipes begin the solos and the whistle joins an octave higher in running semiquavers, with the fiddle using double stopping, accents and triplets in verse 2. African: the kora enters at the end of verse 1 and the talking drum layers into the free-time intro. Western dance: a drum machine, synthesisers, breath samples, electric piano and a looped bass riff. The point is that they sound simultaneously rather than in turn, layered as loops, so the listener hears all three at once.

questions.modelAnswer: The three traditions are present at once rather than in turn, and that simultaneity is what makes the track a fusion rather than a medley. From the **Celtic** side, the **uilleann pipes** open the solo section and the **whistle** joins an octave higher in running semiquavers with occasional **glissando**, while the **fiddle** accompanies verse 2 using **double stopping**, accents and triplets. From **Africa** come the **kora**, entering at the end of verse 1, and the **talking drum**, which layers into the free-time intro. **Western dance** supplies the **drum machine**, the **synthesisers** that hold the opening drone, **breath samples**, **electric piano** and the looped **bass riff** on C and B flat. Because almost everything is a **loop**, these elements can be stacked and removed independently, so a Celtic solo sounds over an African drum and a Western bass line simultaneously. The studio is itself part of the fusion: **reverb** is obvious throughout, a **delay** effect echoes the flute in verse 1, and the intro's two synth tones are **hard-panned and filtered** against each other.

questions.prompt: A student writes: *Release is a Celtic folk song with some electronics added on top.* Evaluate that statement.
questions.solution: There is something in it, because the Celtic element is the most prominent: the uilleann pipes and whistle take the solos, the fiddle accompanies verse 2 with double stopping, and the bodhrán and hurdy-gurdy are heard throughout. But the description fails on two counts. First, the African tradition is not mentioned at all, though the kora and talking drum are both present. Second, calling the electronics an addition on top gets the method backwards: the piece is constructed from loops, and the drum machine, synthesisers, samples and looped bass are structural rather than decorative, with the intro opening with nothing but two filtered, hard-panned synth tones. A fusion combines its traditions so that each remains audible, and here all three do, so the statement is not adequate.

examTechnique.body:
Section A questions on this set work are short and precise: one term for one mark, spelled correctly. Know the facts cold — Simon Emmerson, 1995, Real World Records, Sinéad O'Connor, 25 January 1999, C minor, simple quadruple, three verses and no chorus — so no time goes on recalling them.

For anything longer, the rule is the same every time: name the device, say **which of the three traditions** it belongs to, and say **what it does to the sound**. A list of instruments with no traditions and no effects sits in the bottom band however accurate it is.

Section B sets this against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study. Compare **by element**, both pieces in every paragraph, and end with a judgement. Texture is usually the richest comparison here, because this track moves through homophonic, polyphonic and heterophonic writing while most pop is homophonic throughout.
examinerErrors: Writing about a chorus. There is **no chorus**: three verses, an intro, solos, breaks and an outro.
Listing instruments without saying which tradition each belongs to. The tradition is half the mark.
Calling the texture polyphonic when a decorated version of the same line is heard against the original. That is **heterophonic**.
Treating the electronics as decoration. The piece is **built from loops**, and the intro **opens** with nothing but two filtered synth tones.
Giving the key as C major. It is **C minor**, diatonic but modal.
Saying the piece is in free time throughout. Only the **opening of the intro** is: the steady tempo arrives later in the intro, when the bodhrán, shaker and drum machine enter.
Naming the kora or talking drum as Celtic. They are **African**; the bodhrán, fiddle, whistle, accordion, hurdy-gurdy and uilleann pipes are Celtic.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer attaches every device to one of the three traditions and to an audible effect, and uses *heterophonic* correctly for the decorated pipe loop over the hurdy-gurdy. It knows the structure has no chorus and can trace a single loop, such as the two-note bass riff, entering, dropping out and returning. It explains the intro's technology precisely, two hard-panned synth tones under low pass filters in free time, and it treats the studio as part of the fusion rather than as an afterthought. In Section B it compares element by element with both pieces in every paragraph, ending on a judgement.
